transcript:
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Rylan Barton.
The Supreme Court will allow the Trump administration to continue deporting people to countries
other than their own for now.
While the justice is considered whether the policy is legal, the order lifts for now an
appeals court ruling, which federal attorneys say forced the cancellation of a deportation
flight with about 70 people on board.
The Trump administration has deported some 25,000 people to more than two dozen countries.
Nearly 30 tech executives from Nvidia, OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic gathered at the White
House today for a meeting on AI.
As NPR's Emily Fang reports, many of the executives present have conflicting views on the mounting
concerns about the safety of the technology.
Rather than settle on what should be regulated, President Trump said the meeting leaned towards
letting the AI companies regulate themselves.
Well, there's a belief that there should be tremendous self-regulation, and we automatically
have regulation with the Department of Justice, the FBI, all of that.
Of course, regulators have to make rules before prosecutors can enforce them.
Trump also said they discuss tech companies helping local communities more when they build
data centers.
That might be supplying oil and gas, it might be supplying education.
Data centers are unpopular among the American electorate, but Trump is a strong supporter
of them.
Emily Fang, NPR News, the White House.
President Trump is not permitted to rescind more than $800 million in spending on immigrant
services and diversity-focused initiatives approved by Congress, according to the Government
Accountability Office.
Using the same maneuver he used to defund public radio and TV last year, Trump attempted to
withhold the funds, but this time without congressional approval.
He announced the move last Friday, making congressional action all but impossible, with
just five days left in the federal fiscal year and the House out of session through
the November election.
New York Democratic Governor Kathy Hochul is calling for an outside investigation of
Cornell University's response to an alleged rape case.
From the New York Public News Network, Samuel King reports prosecutors announced they are
reopening a criminal investigation into the incident.
Hochul called the allegations "nothing short of horrifying" and that no student should
be left to wonder whether institutions meant to protect them will listen and act.
In a civil lawsuit, the alleged victim says multiple men drugged and then raped her at
a Cornell fraternity house in 2024.
She also says universities should have known the fraternity chapter had a drug culture.
Cornell says it did a thorough investigation, and the students involved were either expelled
or suspended.
The chapter was barred from campus.
Meanwhile, state lawmakers say they will explore whether changes to sexual assault laws are
needed when they return to the Capitol in January.
For NPR News, I'm Samuel King in Albany.
Americans' confidence in the economy sank to the lowest level in more than a decade this
month as prices remain elevated and wages stagnate amid the Iran War.
It's the lowest reading in the survey since April 2014 and below the lowest level reached
during the pandemic.
This is NPR News.
California Democratic Governor Gavin Newsom has signed a law banning local, state and
federal officers from using gloves that can deliver electric shocks to people.
The ban comes weeks after ICE made plans to give its officers the gloves.
Newsom signed a law last year banning officers from wearing face coverings, but it was blocked
in a federal court.
Texas Republican Governor Greg Abbott has issued a statewide disaster proclamation over
record high diesel prices.
Texas Public Radio's Marianne Navarro has more.
Abbott said soaring diesel prices has put Texas' agricultural and freight industries
at risk.
The 30-day declaration waves dyed diesel restrictions in the state and raises the allowable weight
for fuel, agricultural and timber loads.
Electric diesel is off-road fuel marked red that is typically barred on public roadways.
The declaration also suspends Texas' low emissions diesel rules to the extent authorized
by the Environmental Protection Agency.
Abbott also requested that the EPA waive federal ultra-low sulfur diesel requirements, which
would allow more fuel at the pumps and could reduce prices.
I'm Marianne Navarro in San Antonio.
A journalist has been crowned king of a traditional monarchy that lost its one-time boy king last
month.
The death of King Oyo Ngimba last month triggered a succession dispute in Uganda's Touro Kingdom.
The journalist picked to replace him as a prince who had long been employed as a broadcaster
and editor with Uganda Broadcasting Corp.
He performed rituals overnight, was ushered into the palace, and was formally unveiled
to his followers today.
I'm Rylan Barton.
You're listening to NPR News from Washington.

topics.text: Supreme Court allows Trump administration to continue deporting people to countries other than their own
Tech executives from Nvidia, OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic meet at White House on AI regulation
Government Accountability Office rules Trump cannot rescind $800 million in immigrant services and diversity spending
New York Governor Hochul calls for outside investigation of Cornell University's handling of alleged rape case
Prosecutors reopen criminal investigation into alleged rape at Cornell fraternity house in 2024
Americans' confidence in economy sinks to lowest level in more than a decade
California Governor Newsom signs law banning electric shock gloves for law enforcement officers
Texas Governor Abbott issues disaster proclamation over record high diesel prices affecting agriculture and freight
Journalist crowned king of Uganda's Touro Kingdom following death of previous king last month
